Crypto Scams

Crypto Investment Scam UK: Spot a Fake Platform

Crypto scammers are getting smarter — but you can stay ahead of them by knowing their exact tactics.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-04-21 · Updated 2026-08-01 · 6 min read

Quick answer: Treat a crypto platform promising guaranteed or unusually high returns as a serious scam warning. Check the firm in the FCA's tools, then verify its contact details and permissions because registration is not approval of the investment and clones reuse real firms' details. Never pay an extra fee or tax to unlock a displayed balance, and report losses promptly.
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Use the right recovery route. Follow the payment, account and identity checklist; reporting differs in Scotland.

What a crypto investment scam looks like

A crypto investment scam uses a fake platform, a celebrity endorsement, or a relationship built online to convince you to deposit cryptocurrency into an account you cannot really control. An example of the style is: As seen on TV — this AI-powered crypto platform, endorsed by [celebrity], guarantees 15% monthly returns. Limited spaces available today.

The platform typically shows a rising balance that you can never actually withdraw. This guide shows the warning signs, how to protect yourself, and what to do if you have already invested.

Why these scams are convincing

Fake celebrity endorsements, sometimes using manipulated images, video, or deepfakes, borrow a well-known face's credibility. Slick apps and dashboards showing steady, rising profits look like a genuine trading platform, and contact through social media or a dating app can build weeks of trust before money is mentioned.

The fact that protects you: a promise of guaranteed or unusually high returns is a serious scam warning, and the FCA warns that crypto is high risk — you should be prepared to lose all the money you put in, even where the firm is registered with it.

Signs a crypto investment is a scam

  • It uses a celebrity endorsement or news-style advert you cannot verify independently.
  • It promises guaranteed, fixed, or unusually high returns.
  • The dashboard shows rising profits you can never actually withdraw.
  • You are asked to deposit more to "unlock" a withdrawal or pay a fake tax or fee.
  • The approach came through social media, a dating app, or an unsolicited message.
  • You are pressured to act quickly, or told spaces are limited.
  • A "recovery" service later offers to get your lost money back for a fee. The giveaway variant promises to return more than you send; our Twitter crypto giveaway scam guide covers it.

How the scam works

First, an advert, message, or online relationship introduces the "opportunity". Second, you are shown a platform with a convincing dashboard and encouraged to deposit. Third, the balance appears to grow, encouraging further deposits. Fourth, when you try to withdraw, you are told to pay a fee or tax first, or the platform disappears entirely.

Verifying any platform and any celebrity connection independently before you send money is the only real protection.

How to protect yourself

Treat a platform promising guaranteed or unusually high returns as a serious scam warning, and check it before you deposit anything.

  • Never invest on the strength of a celebrity endorsement without confirming it through that person's own official channels.
  • Look the firm up in the FCA Firm Checker at register.fca.org.uk to see whether it is authorised and has permission for what it is selling you. The FCA's full Financial Services Register carries more detail, including restrictions on crypto activity that the Firm Checker may not show, so read the status, permissions, restrictions and contact details rather than treating a search result as approval of the investment.
  • Checked on 26 July 2026, cryptoasset exchange providers, custodian wallet providers and crypto-ATM operators doing that business in the UK must register with the FCA under the Money Laundering Regulations. That is an anti-money-laundering registration, not approval of the product. The FCA says its new cryptoasset regime under the Financial Services and Markets Act is scheduled to start on 25 October 2027, so check the current position before relying on this.
  • Absence from the register is a warning, not the whole test. Fraudsters also clone authorised firms and quote a genuine firm's real name, address and reference number, so call the firm back on the contact details shown on the register rather than any supplied to you.
  • The FCA says access to the Financial Ombudsman Service or the Financial Services Compensation Scheme is unlikely for most cryptoassets, so do not treat registration as a safety net.
  • Treat an investment recommendation from a new online friend or romantic contact as a serious scam warning, especially where the person directs you to a particular platform or coach.
  • Refuse any payment demanded to unlock your own balance, and keep private keys and recovery phrases to yourself.

If you are unsure, our Pig Butchering Scam UK: Dating Apps & Fake Crypto and Bitcoin Scam UK: Spot a Fake Crypto Investment guides cover the wider crypto-investment pattern in more detail.

If you have already invested

Stop sending money, including any "fee" or "tax" demanded to release a balance, and do not let the platform talk you into one more deposit to fix it. Export or screenshot the account history, the deposit records and the chat before your access is withdrawn — a fake platform can be switched off without notice.

Tell your bank or card issuer how the money left your account, then follow the payment, account and identity steps in the scam recovery checklist.

How to report a crypto investment scam (UK)

Take the right route to the Financial Conduct Authority. A misleading promotion connected to an authorised firm goes through the FCA's financial promotion reporting form. A firm you suspect is unauthorised, or a clone using a real firm's details, goes through the FCA's scam and unauthorised-firm contact route, or its consumer helpline on 0800 111 6768. Say clearly which one you think it is, because a clone is a different investigation from an unregistered platform.

A financial loss also belongs in a fraud report: reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040 for England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and Police Scotland on 101. Forwarding addresses for a scam email or text are listed in the scam recovery checklist.

Frequently asked questions

Is every crypto platform with celebrity backing a scam?

Treat it as high risk. Verify any celebrity endorsement directly through their own official channels, not through the advert or platform itself. Fake endorsements, including deepfakes, are common in crypto scams.

A platform shows my balance growing but I can't withdraw — what does that mean?

This is a classic sign of a fake investment platform. The balance is often not real. Being asked to pay a fee or tax to "release" it is the scam continuing, not a genuine requirement.

Does FCA registration mean a crypto firm is safe?

No. Registration under the Money Laundering Regulations is an anti-money-laundering check on the business, not approval of the investment, and the FCA says access to the Financial Ombudsman Service or the Financial Services Compensation Scheme is unlikely for most cryptoassets. Crypto remains high risk even with a registered firm.

Can I get my money back from a crypto investment scam?

Possibly, but often difficult once crypto has moved on. If you funded the purchase by card, ask your bank about a chargeback. An eligible domestic consumer payment sent by Faster Payments or CHAPS on or after 7 October 2024 may be covered by the mandatory APP reimbursement rules, subject to exclusions, an £85,000 cap, a possible excess of up to £100 that cannot be applied to a consumer the firm assesses as vulnerable, and a 13-month outer reporting limit. Report it immediately rather than relying on that window.

How do I report a crypto investment scam?

Two routes matter. Report a misleading promotion from an authorised firm on the FCA's financial promotion form, and a suspected unauthorised or clone firm through its scam contact route or consumer helpline on 0800 111 6768. A financial loss goes to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk, or to Police Scotland on 101 north of the border.

Fast checks

  • Verify with an official site, app, or number
  • Never share one-time passcodes
  • Be sceptical of bank transfer pressure
